comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
Built and driven: branch e1m0/shared-log @ da14555 (pushed; STACKED on the unmerged e1m0/browser-environment @ 7b8ed80, since the shared side extends that log). 38 checks green (npm run test:e1m0), the repo's existing 11 unchanged.

SHAPE FIRST, as the bead requires, before any writer existed: the log entry gains a kind (act | presence | activity | see) so shared facts live in the SAME log (a second log would make 'the global state is the log' false). One file per root was always shorthand for one file per (root, writer) — one writer per root needs no lock, readers merge by (instance, seq).

SEEN-MARKS (the seam, proved before writers): a mark is a POSITION PER WRITER (version vector) — never a position in 'the merged log', which has no such sequence and would reintroduce the total order the design refuses. Claimed on read, appended, folded by furthest position (so a stale mark never moves a reader backwards); nothing derived returns a globally ordered list — unseenBy is one group per writer, each in that writer's own order.

THE PAIRS THAT WOULD COLLAPSE, both sides asserted: (a) 'has not run yet' (no mark → null = no knowledge) vs 'ran and read nothing' (an empty mark = knowledge); (b) 'never seen' (absent from the presence map) vs 'went quiet' (unreachable, with what it last claimed kept beside it); (c) current work vs a stale claim. Liveness is MEASURED AT READ TIME against windows that are data.

DRIVEN: tests/two-agents.test.mjs — two workers, one project, each seeing the other's presence, activity and read positions with nothing merged (including the collapse pair live, and the page's 'Who is here' panel). HONEST LIMIT stated: two workers share OPFS by construction, so this proves the LOG's semantics, not a transport between machines (E2, unbuilt).

TWO DEFECTS THE DRIVE FOUND (both invisible while one agent existed): a look claimed its marks BEFORE reporting, so unseen was always empty and the work just caught up on was invisible; and auditAll read only this instance's file per root, so a second agent's log could not be merged at all. title: An extension surface: discover, inventory, sideload — and the disclosure between them
description: Paul's N17: 'some user interface to tell the user what extensions exist, what extensions are installed, how to maybe sideload extensions that someone else has made.' Three verbs, not equally hard: DISCOVER (what exists - implies a registry or catalogue, and what a stranger's extension looks like before installation); INVENTORY (what is installed and where it came from, showing each extension's DECLARED capabilities against its ENFORCED ones - the distinction the whole design rests on); SIDELOAD (the highest-reach act a user can perform in this system, because an extension runs exactly where the agent runs - so a confirm-first act whose resolved plan is the extension's source, and the host owns the admission point; a paste must not reload its own proposal). Plus the surface Paul did not name: THE DISCLOSURE - what this extension can reach, what it will be given, and what it cannot have. Suggested to astra as a prototype target because it is where the security model becomes something a person can see. Owner: astra (study scope), unassigned for the real build.

title: Prove the extension system can express MCP servers and web search (Paul's stress tests)
description: Paul's N16, framed by him as tests rather than a backlog: 'maybe they're a stress test for how the extensions can work.' Skills are NOT first-class - capabilities are extensions, and both the user and the model arrive at the same admission point (docs/02-environment.md 1.7). Two concrete tests with different failure modes: WEB SEARCH forces capabilities to be able to say 'network' and bounds to say 'how much' - nothing in the feature list exercises either field today, so if the vocabulary cannot express it that is a small, early, field-level failure. AN MCP SERVER forces placement and authority - a tool whose implementation is another PROCESS means the model authors a LAUNCH, not a function, which is a strictly larger authority question than the registration gap, and it forces 'authority when execution is remote from the decision' because an MCP server is by definition somewhere else. Ordering from qwen2's harvest: web search tells you whether the vocabulary is rich enough; an MCP server tells you whether the architecture is.

INDEPENDENT REVIEW of feat/extension-admission @ 40a030c5 (reviewer: lane CHANNEL, a different model family). Verdict: PASS on six of the seven claims, with ONE enforcement finding. Full report: ~/journal/reports/2026-09-20-voicebox-extension-admission-review.md.

THE FINDING — the mediated fetch checks the FIRST URL, then lets fetch follow redirects (lib/extensions.mjs:273 checks, :284 fetches). Driven: a tool whose bounds.hosts is ["127.0.0.1"] was pointed at my own declared host, which answered 302 -> http://localhost:8800/api/extensions (localhost is NOT declared). The call returned the body served by the undeclared host while reporting host "127.0.0.1". Three observed consequences: (1) the admission disclosure says the tool "gets" a mediated fetch that refuses unlisted hosts "by name" — true of the initial URL, not of where the bytes came from; (2) the budget counts CALLS, not hops — one call that made two requests counted 1/3; (3) the audit entry records act.target as the declared URL and observed.bytes 8577 served by localhost, so a followed redirect is invisible. Fix shape is the author's call; `redirect: "manual"` with a named refusal for a 3xx, or re-check Location per hop and charge each hop.

comments.text:
INDEPENDENT REVIEW of c6b3b823 (the wire shapes; reviewer: lane CHANNEL, different model family from the author). Verdict: PASS on all four claims, with ONE defect in a pure function. Report: ~/journal/reports/2026-09-20-voicebox-wire-shapes-review.md. Suite re-run by me: 58/58.

THE DEFECT — core/wire.ts:101: parseCall's object branch tests the uninitialised `obj` instead of `raw` (`} else if (obj && typeof raw === "object") {`), so EVERY object argument is refused as "malformed-call" / "the call is not an object" — including a good call. Driven both ways with the same data: an object (even one smuggling decision:"allow") -> malformed-call; the same data as a JSON string -> unknown-field (correct). Latent on the wire (strings), NOT latent for this commit's own framing: the in-process round trip. ExecutorDoor.receive makes it visible rather than better — it JSON.parses a copy for the callId probe (lib/channel.mjs:106) but passes the ORIGINAL raw to parseCall, so the door's stringify never reaches the parser. One word to fix at :101 (obj -> raw); parseAnswer:157 does it correctly (`raw && typeof raw === "object"`), so the typo is singular.

VERIFIED, DRIVEN: (1) envelopes — good call ok=true with observed ["action","content"]; tampered boundsEcho -> bounds-mismatch with the why QUOTING the admitted bounds ("hosts":["127.0.0.1"]) so a routed call cannot carry its own bounds past the echo and the gate underneath is the one I verified at 0ddba0a5; forged descriptorId -> unattributed-call; missing boundsEcho -> unattributed-call. THE BONUS HOLDS: a descriptor refused at admission (mcp-server-local, exec-absent) is not in the registry, so a call naming it refuses unattributed-call ("no admitted descriptor 'mcp-server-local' carrying tool 'mcp_list_tools'") — the refusal bites before an executor exists; I tried its real tool name and its own fields as boundsEcho and both land on the same named refusal. (2) channel contract — an unconnected peer refuses no-page in words and sends ZERO messages; four bad answers (garbage, a valid answer for another callId, an answer smuggling grant:"everything", ok with no observed) NONE settled the pending call (waiting() stayed 1) and the real answer then settled it; an inaudible peer gives an honest page-timeout rather than a wrong success; abandon() settles with machine-closed. (3) the vocabulary — six names, all distinct AND distinct in what a caller can act on: no-page, machine-unreachable, page-timeout, machine-timeout, page-closed, machine-closed. (4) the boundary — decision:"allow" on a call -> unknown-field, grant:"everything" on an answer -> unknown-field, ok with no observed -> malformed-answer.

NOT REPORTED AS A DEFECT: no live transport endpoint (deliberate), and the peer-parameterisation is real — the same envelopes, validators and vocabulary carried my stand-in peer over a captured pipe.

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text:
A build spec now exists for this bead — not just the existence proof.

`docs/04-e1-m0-build-spec.md` (in the design branch, PR #1) turns §1.8's "what makes the environment real" into what to build: the module layout with the pure `core/`; the browser project record and what *identity is placement + location* means when location is a handle (an OPFS path means nothing outside its origin, so two browsers holding `atlas` are two projects and no code should try to match them); the tier table as **data**, including the rules M0 must have and the ones a browser satisfies **structurally** so they must not be re-implemented; the audit entry shape with per-instance sequencing and **one file per root** (which is how two roots write without interleaving); "create an asset" step by step; and the Wasm answer.

The two things most likely to save the implementer a day:

- **The Wasm module is a 30-line hand-written `.wat` with exactly two imports** (`writeFile`, `note`). No toolchain, no `wasm-pack`. It comes **first** because it is what makes the network row structural rather than promised — and if it slips, the fallback is **not** a JS tool: a JS tool in a worker keeps ambient `fetch`, which makes §1.8's fourth condition false, and the honest fallback is to say the environment does not exist yet.
- **Eight acceptance checks, each with its positive control**, including the two that catch the failure modes already found in this project: `..` as a **name** (not just a path segment), and a test module that imports `fetch` **failing to instantiate** rather than being caught by a policy.

§7 of the spec lists what is **not** designed yet, so it can be treated as a hole rather than interpreted.

title: Every lane worktree prints 'fatal: Needed a single revision' on boot — rev-parse of a branch with no upstream
description:
FILED BY coord's instruction (voicebox-ui, 2026-09-24), from a real gate refusal.

THE OBSERVATION, in coord's words as asked: a check that resolves a revision it cannot resolve is the same family as everything else tonight.

WHERE IT COMES FROM: two call sites resolve the remote-tracking ref for the CURRENT branch:
  · server.mjs:916 (the build payload: branch/remote/ahead/dirty)
  · vite.config.js:79 (the page's build stamp)
Both run `git rev-parse --short origin/<branch>`. In a WORKTREE WHOSE BRANCH HAS NO UPSTREAM — which is every lane worktree before its first push — that command writes:

    fatal: Needed a single revision

to stderr on EVERY boot. Seen twice today: in the served server's own log (hours before this bead), and in the scratch server's captured stderr inside the f0b denylist test, where it was the only diagnostic next to a probe that had died.

IS IT LOAD-BEARING? CHECKED, and the answer is NO — both sites pass a default (`git([...], "")`) and both handle the empty result: the stamp says 'no origin/<branch> here, so the distance from a remote is unknown', and the health payload reports `remote: null, ahead: null`. So nothing is failing quietly; the cost is NOISE, and noise in a server's stderr is exactly what makes a reader mistake it for a fault (it appeared in this evening's gate refusal, next to an unrelated SocketError).

THE FIX, one line at each site: use the idiomatic existence test — `git rev-parse --quiet --verify origin/<branch>` — which exits 1 with NO stderr when the ref is absent, so the intent ('does this ref exist?') is explicit instead of being read off a default, and the 'fatal:' line disappears from every lane worktree's boot. Keep the existing fallbacks; this only stops git complaining.

NOT URGENT, and filed rather than fixed because coord asked for the filing and because the two sites are shared infrastructure (the stamp is a surface every lane reads).
close_reason: landed on origin/main: cherry-pick f704483 (quiet --verify --short rev-parse in server.mjs and vite.config.js), verified in the tree (both call sites present) and by patch-id equivalence with fe522af. title: wasm call fan-out: a concurrency semaphore for worker-holding calls — IF turn volume justifies it
description: A NAMED COST, measured not guessed (vb-resolver, 2026-09-23, feat/wasm-bounds): wasm calls each hold a worker for up to the host deadline, and there is NO concurrency cap — 20 parallel loop-calls held 20 spinning workers, Δ158MB RSS. The live batch path is serialized per session, but HTTP turns are not: N requests hold N workers for the deadline. DO NOT BUILD until the condition holds: turn volume where concurrent wasm calls are routine (measured, not anticipated) — e.g. sustained >50 concurrent wasm-holding turns, or one observed incident. THEN: a semaphore in lib/wasm-shelf.mjs's runInWorker (a small in-process counter + queue) capping concurrent workers, excess calls refused over-budget by name rather than queued unboundedly. Until then the cost is named in the gate's admission gets[] and the module header.

title: Compiled modules are compared by comments and strings — a code-only edit is invisible there
description:
DELIBERATE LIMIT of the currency check as landed (voicebox-beads-590, reviewed by vb-resolver 2026-09-23). tools/served-vs-disk.mjs compares a compiled .ts module (the server strips types and rewrites imports) by its COMMENT lines and its STRING LITERALS of 8+ characters — measured on browser/ui/ui.ts: 540 of 582 disk lines appear in the served copy, while comments (100/100) and strings (142/142) survive. vb-resolver verified the limit independently: drifting acts.ts 2000 -> 2500 was NOT caught, as the message states.

WHY NOT TIGHTER, and this is the interesting part: a type-stripping comparison (strip annotations from both sides, then compare) would catch code-only edits, but any mismatch between two strippers produces a FALSE RED on every run — and a gate that false-reds every run is worse than a named-narrow one, because people learn to ignore it. The limit is stated in the failure message ('a change that touches neither is not visible here') rather than left implied.

THE FOLLOW-UP, IF ANYONE WANTS IT: type-strip with the SAME transformer the server uses (not a second implementation), so the comparison is exact for both sides, and prove it against the real browser/ui/ui.ts and core/*.ts before wiring it in. Until then this bead is the record that the gap is known, named, and chosen.
close_reason:
FIXED — branch fix/compiled-module-exact @ 2324aa3, pushed (gate clear), awaiting the merger's landing.

TWO DEFECTS WERE STACKED, and the second was the bigger one — which is why the repro I filed (a code-only edit is invisible) was only half the story:

1. THE COMPARISON WAS NOT EXACT. The server serves a .ts module as stripTypeScriptTypes(readFileSync(file), { mode: 'strip' }), so the check now computes that same output for the disk file and compares it with the server's OWN CALL rather than a second implementation that could disagree with the first. Measured before choosing: strip-then-compare is byte-identical for browser/ui/ui.ts, browser/acts.ts, core/paths.ts, core/root.ts. A failure names the difference: 'acts.ts: the front is not serving what this tree compiles to — first difference at line 83: this tree compiles to "const LIST_LIMIT = 250;" and the front serves "const LIST_LIMIT = 200;"'. The comments-and-strings rule is now the FALLBACK (runtime without a stripper), exported and pinned by a test rather than a branch nobody exercises.

2. THE WALK NEVER REACHED THE FILE. Only .js refs were followed, so a compiled module's imports were never fetched at all — and nothing pointed at the worker: it is constructed at runtime (new Worker('/browser/worker.ts')), so browser/worker.ts AND ITS WHOLE GRAPH (browser/acts.ts, browser/opfs.ts, …) went uncompared. Measured: 8 modules compared; with the walk fixed, 12. So the code-only edit to acts.ts was invisible because the check never saw the file — the comparison was right and unexercised. The walk now follows .ts/.mjs imports and both worker forms.

DRIVEN BOTH DIRECTIONS in an environment of the branch's own (api :8899, front :5221, never Paul's), with a scratch tree at the SAME sha as the front's so identity matched: a code-only edit (acts.ts LIST_LIMIT 200 -> 250, no comment and no string touched) -> FAILS quoting both values and the line; the same tree unmutated -> PASS, 12 modules compared. And the counterfactual is now measured rather than argued: the fallback rule, handed the same pair, says nothing about the constant — it reports comments lost to type-stripping instead, a false positive of its own, which is a second reason it is the fallback and not the rule.

AND A PROPERTY WORTH KEEPING FROM THE PUSH: it went through. With the identity half composed into 590, a lane whose tree is not the one on the front now SKIPS BY NAME rather than failing — so the strict content rule blocks only when the front serves YOUR tree and your files differ, which is real lag. That is the composed design working, and it corrects my earlier statement to coord that the stricter rule would block side-worktree pushes.

title: A present-not-admitted file has no direct admit door — the host must stage then admit
description:
Found by the lane that closed bxx (2026-09-20), as a cosmetic lifecycle note rather than a gate.

A file that is PRESENT-NOT-ADMITTED has no direct admit door: the host must first stage it as a
proposal and then admit the proposal. It works, the outcome is correct, and every refusal is
named — but the host has to perform a two-step dance for a file it can already see.

The smoother shape: a host-side convenience that admits a file it can already name as present —
"admit this present file" — going through the SAME host token and the SAME ledger, so the
audit trail is identical and no new authority is introduced. Not a security change: the host
already holds the token that admits.

Small, and worth doing while the shape is fresh in the mind of whoever last drove it.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: Paul Kinlan
comments.text: DONE — feat/present-admit-door @33e2b51 (pushed; repo pre-push gate + page acceptance ALL CLEAR). The direct door: admitProposal falls back to the host directory when no proposal exists — same route, same host token (token-less admit refuses host-token-required), same gate re-run, same ledger (the admission is recorded). deny in place appends a ledger deny entry and the file stays present-not-admitted, never live. The inventory's present list is computed from directory + ledger AT CALL TIME, so a mid-session drop is visible immediately without waiting for a reload (that state gap was found by this drive and fixed). GET .../plan discloses a present file before the decision. Tests: the t9j drive in tests/extensions.test.mjs; whole gate 198/198 + acceptance ALL CLEAR.
